lessons.title: Forms of Energy and Their Daily Applications

pages.body:
Think about everything that has happened since you woke up this morning. You ate breakfast (chemical energy). You walked to school (kinetic energy). The sun warmed your face (solar energy). You are sitting under electric lights (electrical and light energy). You can hear your teacher (sound energy).

- How many forms of energy can you identify in your daily routine?
- Where does the energy that powers a generator ultimately come from?

> **DEFINITION** **Energy:** the ability to do work or cause a change. Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another.

[[img:i0l7a20v0]]

pages.body:
| **Form of energy** | **What it is** | **Everyday examples in Ghana** |
|---|---|---|
| Potential Energy (PE) | Stored energy due to an object's position or state. Gained when an object is lifted or stretched. | Water stored in the Akosombo dam; a coconut at the top of a palm tree; a bent catapult |
| Kinetic Energy (KE) | Energy of motion. Any moving object has kinetic energy. | A trotro moving on the road; a ball rolling; flowing water in a river; a ceiling fan spinning |
| Heat (Thermal) Energy | Energy produced by the vibration of particles. Flows from hotter to cooler objects. | Cooking on a wood fire or gas stove; warmth of the Sun; a hot engine; friction between car brakes |
| Sound Energy | Energy carried by vibrations through a medium. Cannot travel through a vacuum. | Drumming at a festival; a school bell; speaking and hearing; traffic noise |
| Solar Energy | Energy produced by the Sun as electromagnetic radiation. | Sunlight warming homes; solar panels on rooftops; drying crops, fish and meat in the sun |
| Electrical Energy | Energy carried by moving electrons through a conductor. | ECG power supply to homes; torch batteries; phone chargers; electric fans |
| Chemical Energy | Energy stored in the chemical bonds of a substance. Released by chemical reactions. | Food we eat; firewood and charcoal; petrol; dry cell batteries; explosives |
| Light Energy | Energy carried as electromagnetic waves that can be detected by the human eye. | Sunlight; LED torches; candles; kerosene lamps; phone screens; vehicle headlights |
| Nuclear Energy | Energy stored in the nucleus of atoms. Released by nuclear fission or fusion. | The Sun's core (nuclear fusion); nuclear power stations in some countries |

pages.body:
Hold a stone above the ground and release it. Before you let go, the stone was still but had energy stored in it because of its height. As it fell, it moved faster and faster.

- Where did the movement energy come from?
- Would a heavier stone have more or less energy at the same height? Why?
- Would the same stone dropped from higher up have more or less kinetic energy when it reaches the ground?

[[img:i6hoj8051]]

pages.title: Potential Energy (PE)
pages.body:
Gravitational Potential Energy is the energy an object has because of its height above a reference point (usually the ground). The higher the object and the heavier it is, the more PE it stores.

> **DEFINITION** **Gravitational Potential Energy:** the energy stored in an object due to its height above the ground. Formula: PE = mgh, where m = mass (kg), g = gravitational field strength (10 N/kg on Earth) and h = height (m).

questions.q: A 6 kg box is lifted to a height of 8 m. Calculate its potential energy. (g = 10 N/kg)

ideas.t: Uses PE = mgh
Answer 480 J

questions.q: A 5 kg rock is held 4 m above the ground. What is its gravitational potential energy? (g = 10 N/kg)
questions.e: Potential Energy (PE) Gravitational Potential Energy is the energy an object has because of its height above a reference point (usually the ground).

questions.q: State the formula for PE and the formula for KE. For each formula, identify what every symbol stands for.

parts.a: PE = mgh where m is mass in kg, g is gravitational field strength (10 N/kg) and h is height in m. KE = ½mv² where m is mass in kg and v is speed in m/s.

ideas.t: PE = mgh
m is mass, g is gravitational field strength, h is height
KE = ½mv²
v is speed or velocity

pages.title: Factors affecting Potential Energy
pages.body:
- Mass (m): a heavier object at the same height has more PE. A bag of cocoa at the top of a lorry has more PE than a small stone at the same height.
- Height (h): the same object at a greater height has more PE. A bucket of water at the top of a three-storey building has more PE than the same bucket at the second floor.
- Gravity (g): on the Moon, where gravity is weaker (about 1.6 N/kg instead of 10 N/kg), the same object at the same height would have much less PE.

pages.title: Kinetic Energy (KE)
pages.body:
Kinetic Energy is the energy an object has because it is moving. The faster it moves, the more KE it has. Note that speed has a squared effect, so doubling the speed quadruples the KE.

> **DEFINITION** **Kinetic Energy:** the energy of a moving object. Formula: KE = ½mv², where m = mass (kg) and v = velocity or speed (m/s).

questions.q: Two vehicles travel at the same speed. One has a mass of 1,000 kg and the other has a mass of 5,000 kg. Which has more kinetic energy, and by how much?

parts.a: The 5000 kg vehicle has more kinetic energy, five times as much, because KE is proportional to mass (5000 ÷ 1000 = 5).

ideas.t: The 5000 kg vehicle has more KE
It has five times as much

pages.title: Factors affecting Kinetic Energy
pages.body:
- Mass (m): a heavy lorry moving at the same speed as a motorcycle has far more KE. This is why lorries cause much more damage in crashes.
- Speed (v): speed is squared in the formula. Doubling speed gives four times the KE. A car at 100 km/h has four times the KE of the same car at 50 km/h. This is why speeding is so dangerous.

pages.title: Mechanical Energy and conservation
pages.body:
When a ball is held up and released, its Potential Energy converts to Kinetic Energy as it falls. At any point during the fall, the total Mechanical Energy (PE + KE) remains constant, assuming no friction or air resistance. This is an application of the Law of Conservation of Energy.

Mechanical Energy = PE + KE = constant

questions.q: Explain, using the concept of mechanical energy, what happens to the PE and KE of a football as it is kicked upward and then falls back down.

parts.a: As the ball rises its KE changes into PE; at the top it has maximum PE; as it falls the PE changes back into KE. The total mechanical energy (PE + KE) stays constant if there is no air resistance.

ideas.t: Going up, kinetic energy changes into potential energy
Falling, potential energy changes back into kinetic energy
Total mechanical energy (PE + KE) stays constant

pages.title: Worked Examples
pages.body:
Example 1: A 4 kg rock is held 5 m above the ground. Calculate its PE. (g = 10 N/kg)

PE = mgh = 4 × 10 × 5 = 200 J

Example 2: A 3 kg ball is moving at 6 m/s. Calculate its KE.

KE = ½mv² = ½ × 3 × 6² = ½ × 3 × 36 = 54 J

Example 3: A 5 kg ball is dropped from 10 m. What is its KE just before it hits the ground? (g = 10 N/kg)

PE at top = mgh = 5 × 10 × 10 = 500 J. All PE converts to KE. Therefore KE at bottom = 500 J.

Example 4: A 2 kg stone is dropped from rest. Its KE just before hitting the ground is 160 J. From what height was it dropped? (g = 10 N/kg)

PE = KE, so mgh = 160. h = 160 ÷ (2 × 10) = 160 ÷ 20 = 8 m.

> **Doubling the speed of a vehicle gives it FOUR times the kinetic energy, because speed is squared in the formula. This is why road safety campaigns emphasise speed limits: a small increase in speed causes a large increase in the kinetic energy that must be absorbed in a crash.**

questions.q: A 4 kg ball is moving at 5 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

parts.a: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 4 × 25 = 50 J.

ideas.t: Uses KE = ½mv²
Answer 50 J

questions.q: A 10 kg block is dropped from 12 m. What is its KE just before it hits the ground? (Assume all PE converts to KE; g = 10 N/kg)

parts.a: PE at the top = 10 × 10 × 12 = 1200 J. All of it changes to KE, so KE = 1200 J.

ideas.t: PE at the top = mgh

questions.q: A 8 kg mass is dropped from rest at a height of 5 m. Calculate its PE at the top and its KE just before it hits the ground. (g = 10 N/kg)

parts.a: PE at the top = 8 × 10 × 5 = 400 J. All of it changes to KE, so KE just before hitting the ground = 400 J.

ideas.t: PE at the top is 400 J
KE just before the ground is 400 J

ideas.t: PE is 1000 J

pages.body:
On a sunny afternoon, stand outside for a minute. You can feel the sun warming you. Now place a metal spoon in a cup of hot tea. A few seconds later the handle becomes warm. Finally, notice that the air above a coal pot is warm even though you are not touching the pot.

- In each of the three situations above, heat moved from somewhere. Where did it come from?
- Did the heat travel the same way in all three situations, or differently?
- Why does a plastic spoon handle stay cooler than a metal spoon in the same hot cup?

pages.title: What is heat energy?
pages.body: > **DEFINITION** **Heat energy:** a form of energy associated with the vibration of particles in a substance. Heat flows naturally from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature. **Temperature:** a measure of how hot or cold an object is, measured in degrees Celsius (°C) or Kelvin (K). Temperature tells us the average kinetic energy of the particles.

pages.title: Sources of heat energy
pages.body:
Heat energy comes from many natural and artificial (man-made) sources.

**Natural sources of heat**
- The Sun: the main natural source of heat on Earth. Solar radiation warms the ground, water bodies and the atmosphere.
- Geothermal energy: heat from within the Earth, released through volcanoes, hot springs and geysers.
- Lightning: extremely hot electrical discharge that heats the air around it.
- Friction in nature: heat generated when rocks slide against each other during earthquakes.
- Chemical reactions in living things: the human body generates heat through metabolic processes.

**Artificial (man-made) sources of heat**
- Burning fuels: firewood, charcoal, gas, kerosene and petrol release heat when burned.
- Electrical heating: electric cookers, electric irons, electric kettles and heaters convert electrical energy to heat.
- Friction: rubbing two surfaces together generates heat (e.g. lighting a match, braking).
- Nuclear reactors: nuclear fission produces large amounts of heat in power stations.
- Exothermic chemical reactions: reactions that release heat, such as the setting of cement.

pages.title: Methods of heat transfer
pages.body:
Heat energy always moves from a hotter region to a cooler one. It does so by three methods: conduction, convection and radiation.

[[img:ihwooxem2]]

| **Method** | **How it works** | **Medium needed** | **Everyday examples** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conduction | Particles in a hot region vibrate more energetically and pass this vibration to neighbouring particles. Heat travels through the material particle by particle, without the material itself moving. | Solid (usually) | A metal cooking pot heating on a fire; a metal spoon getting hot in tea; iron roofing sheet heating in the sun; hot engine parts |
| Convection | A heated fluid (liquid or gas) expands, becomes less dense, rises, cools, becomes denser and sinks, creating a circulation loop called a convection current. | Liquid or gas (fluid) | Boiling water circulating in a pot; warm air rising from a coal pot heating a room; sea breezes at the coast; ventilation of buildings |
| Radiation | Heat is transmitted as infrared electromagnetic waves. It requires no medium and can travel through a vacuum. | No medium needed | Warmth of the Sun felt from millions of kilometres away; heat from a fire felt across a gap; electric grills and infrared heaters |

questions.q: Describe how heat is transferred by conduction, using the example of a metal spoon in hot soup.

parts.a: The particles of the spoon in the hot soup vibrate more energetically and pass the vibration to neighbouring particles, so heat travels along the spoon particle by particle without the spoon moving.

ideas.t: Particles in the hot part vibrate more
They pass the vibration to neighbouring particles
Heat travels along the material without it moving

questions.q: Explain how a convection current forms in a room heated on one side.

parts.a: The air next to the heater expands, becomes less dense and rises. It cools, becomes denser and sinks, and a circulation loop called a convection current forms.

ideas.t: Heated air expands and becomes less dense
It rises, then cools, becomes denser and sinks
A circulation loop (convection current) forms

questions.q: Which method of heat transfer requires no medium?
questions.e: Radiation: transfer of heat as infrared electromagnetic waves; needs no medium.

questions.q: Describe the three methods of heat transfer and give one example of each.

parts.a: Conduction: particle vibration in solids, e.g. a hot metal spoon. Convection: a heated fluid rises and sinks in a current, e.g. boiling water. Radiation: infrared waves that need no medium, e.g. the Sun's heat.

ideas.t: Conduction: particles vibrate and pass the vibration to neighbours in a solid
Convection: a heated fluid rises, cools and sinks in a circulation
Radiation: infrared waves that need no medium
One example of each

lessons.title: The thermos flask: using all three modes of heat transfer

pages.body: > **DEFINITION** **Conduction:** transfer of heat through a material by particle vibration, without the material itself moving. **Convection:** transfer of heat by the movement of a fluid (liquid or gas) that carries heat with it. **Radiation:** transfer of heat as infrared electromagnetic waves; needs no medium. **Conductor:** a material that allows heat (or electricity) to flow through it easily. Metals are good conductors. **Insulator:** a material that resists the flow of heat. Plastic, wood and air are good insulators.

pages.title: The thermos flask: using all three modes of heat transfer
pages.body:
A thermos flask is designed to keep a hot liquid hot (or a cold liquid cold) for many hours. It does this by reducing or eliminating all three methods of heat transfer at the same time. This makes it an excellent real-world illustration of all three modes working together.

[[img:i1c2bles3]]

questions.q: A student tests three materials (metal, wood, plastic) by placing one end of each in hot water and observing how quickly the other end becomes warm. Predict the order from fastest to slowest heating and explain your reasoning.

parts.a: Metal heats fastest, then wood, then plastic is slowest, because metals are good conductors and wood and plastic are insulators.

ideas.t: Metal is the fastest because it is a good conductor
Wood and plastic are slower because they are insulators

pages.body:
| **Heat transfer method** | **How it is reduced in the thermos flask** |
|---|---|
| Conduction | The double glass walls are poor conductors of heat. The vacuum between them removes the only medium through which conduction could occur. |
| Convection | The vacuum between the glass walls contains no particles. With no fluid present, convection currents cannot form. The liquid inside cannot lose heat this way. |
| Radiation | The inner surfaces of both glass walls are coated with a silvery reflective material. This reflects radiant heat back into the flask rather than allowing it to escape. |
| Conduction through top | The stopper or cork at the top is made of a poor conductor such as rubber or plastic, reducing the small amount of heat that could conduct through the opening. |

> **A thermos flask does not produce heat. It simply prevents heat from escaping. The vacuum is the most important feature: without a medium, neither conduction nor convection can occur. Radiation is reduced by the silver coating, making all three modes minimised simultaneously.**

questions.q: Explain why a thermos flask keeps hot tea hot for many hours, referring to all three methods of heat transfer.

parts.a: It reduces all three modes of heat transfer: the vacuum between the double glass walls prevents conduction and convection, the silvery coating reflects radiation back, and the stopper is a poor conductor.

ideas.t: Conduction is reduced because the double glass walls are poor conductors and the vacuum has no particles
Convection is reduced because the vacuum has no fluid so no convection currents form
Radiation is reduced because the silvery coating reflects heat back
The stopper is a poor conductor

questions.q: A builder wants to keep a concrete roof cool in Ghana's hot climate. She can choose a dark metal roof or a white concrete roof. Which would you recommend and why? Refer to radiation and reflection.

parts.a: Choose the white concrete roof. White surfaces reflect most of the sun's radiation, but a dark metal roof absorbs more radiation and conducts heat into the building.

ideas.t: A white concrete roof is better
It reflects more sunlight (radiation) so it stays cooler
A dark metal roof absorbs more heat and is a good conductor

pages.title: Practical activity: comparing heat conductors
pages.body:
Materials needed: metal rod, plastic rod, wooden stick, glass rod, bowl of hot water, small pieces of butter or wax, a stopwatch.

1. Attach a small piece of butter to one end of each rod.
2. Place all rods with their other ends in hot water at the same time.
3. Time how long it takes the butter to melt on each rod. Record in a table: Material, Time for butter to melt, Good conductor or poor conductor?
4. Rank the materials from best to worst conductor.
5. Write a conclusion explaining why some materials conducted heat faster than others.

Close your eyes in a dark room. You see nothing. Open them or turn on a torch. Immediately you see the walls, furniture and people around you. Light makes vision possible. But what exactly is light, and where does it come from?

- List all the sources of light you can think of, both natural (from nature) and artificial (made by humans).
- Does light travel instantly from source to eye, or does it take time?

pages.title: What is light?
pages.body: > **DEFINITION** **Light energy:** a form of electromagnetic radiation that can be detected by the human eye. Light is a transverse wave that can travel through a vacuum at a speed of approximately 3 × 10⁸ metres per second (300,000 km/s). It carries energy from its source to wherever it travels. **Luminous object:** an object that produces and emits its own light. **Non-luminous object:** an object that does not produce its own light but can be seen because it reflects light from a luminous source.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a luminous object and a non-luminous object. Give two examples of each.

parts.a: A luminous object produces its own light (the Sun, a candle flame); a non-luminous object makes no light of its own and is seen only because it reflects light (the Moon, a mirror).

ideas.t: A luminous object makes its own light
Examples: Sun, candle, bulb, stars
A non-luminous object is seen by reflecting light
Examples: Moon, mirror, book, table

questions.q: Which of the following is a natural source of light?
questions.e: The Sun: the primary source of all natural light on Earth.

questions.q: Define light energy and state whether the following are luminous or non-luminous: the Moon, a candle flame, a mirror, the Sun.

parts.a: Light energy is electromagnetic radiation detected by the eye. The Moon is non-luminous, a candle flame is luminous, a mirror is non-luminous and the Sun is luminous.

ideas.t: Light energy is electromagnetic radiation that the eye can detect
The Moon and the mirror are non-luminous
The candle flame and the Sun are luminous

pages.title: Sources of light energy
pages.body:
**Natural sources of light**
- The Sun: the primary source of all natural light on Earth. All daylight comes from sunlight.
- Stars: distant suns that produce their own light through nuclear fusion.
- Lightning: a very brief but very intense natural electrical discharge.
- Fire: burning produces light as well as heat. Campfires and bush fires are natural fire light.
- Bioluminescence: some living things produce their own light, such as certain deep-sea fish, fireflies and some fungi.

**Artificial (man-made) sources of light**
- Incandescent bulbs: a thin wire (filament) heated by electricity until it glows.
- Fluorescent lamps: electrically excited gas produces ultraviolet rays that cause the coating inside the tube to glow (emit visible light).
- LED lamps: the most energy-efficient electric light, widely used for homes and torches.
- Kerosene lamps and candles: burning hydrocarbons produce light. Still common in rural Ghana without regular electricity.
- Neon signs, lasers and glow sticks: used in advertising, industry and medical applications.

questions.q: Name three natural and three artificial sources of light. For each source, explain how the light is produced.

parts.a: Natural: the Sun, stars, lightning, fire. Artificial: incandescent bulb (filament heated until it glows), fluorescent lamp, LED lamp, candle or kerosene lamp.

ideas.t: Natural source such as the Sun, stars, lightning, fire or fireflies
A second natural source

pages.title: Properties of light energy
pages.body:
Light has several important physical properties that distinguish it from other forms of energy. All of these properties have practical applications in daily life.

| **Property** | **Explanation** | **Evidence or example** |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation) | Light travels only in straight paths called rays. It cannot bend around corners. | Shadows form behind opaque objects; you cannot see around a corner; a torch beam is straight |
| 2. Travels at very high speed | In a vacuum, light travels at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s (300,000 km per second). It slows slightly when entering denser media. | Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth from the Sun, which is 150 million km away |
| 3. Travels through a vacuum | Unlike sound, light does not need a medium. It can travel through empty space. | We receive light and heat from the Sun through the vacuum of space |
| 4. Can be reflected | When light hits a smooth, shiny surface, it bounces back. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. | Mirrors; calm water surfaces; highly polished metal; periscopes |
| 5. Can be refracted (bent) | Light changes direction (bends) when it passes from one medium into another of different density. | A straight stick appears bent in a glass of water; lenses in spectacles and cameras; rainbows |
| 6. Can be dispersed into colours | White light is a mixture of all visible colours. A prism or water droplets separate these colours. | Rainbows; prism experiments; CDs and DVDs showing colour patterns |
| 7. Is a transverse wave | Light vibrates at right angles to its direction of travel. It can be polarised. | Polarising sunglasses reduce glare from reflective surfaces |
| 8. Can be absorbed | Some materials absorb light and convert it to heat or other forms of energy. Dark surfaces absorb more; light surfaces reflect more. | Black clothes feel hotter in sunlight than white clothes; black solar panels absorb sunlight |
| 9. Can undergo total internal reflection | When light hits the boundary inside a denser medium at a large enough angle, all light is reflected back inside. | Optical fibres for internet and phone communication; diamonds (sparkle from total internal reflection) |
| 10. Travels in straight lines to cast shadows | An opaque object blocks light and casts a dark region (shadow) behind it. | Shadows from trees, buildings, your own body in sunlight or lamplight |

pages.title: Rays and beams of light
pages.body:
[[img:ifk64d3c4]]

| **Term** | **Definition** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| Ray | A single line drawn to represent the direction in which light travels. An arrow shows the direction. | In a diagram, a line with an arrowhead showing direction |
| Beam | A collection of many rays from the same source. | A torch beam; sunlight passing through a small gap |

pages.body:
Hold a mirror in front of you and look at your reflection. Now look at your reflection in still water in a bowl. Both show a reversed image. Now look at a rough whitewashed wall in sunlight: you can see the wall is bright, but there is no clear image. Why?

- Why does a smooth mirror give a clear image but a rough wall does not?

[[img:ikz49l0j5]]

> **DEFINITION** **Reflection:** the process in which light bounces back from a surface. The surface must be smooth and shiny for clear (regular) reflection. **Incident ray:** the ray of light hitting the surface. **Reflected ray:** the ray of light bouncing back from the surface. **Normal:** an imaginary line drawn at right angles (90°) to the reflecting surface at the point where light hits. Angles of incidence and reflection are always measured from the normal. **Angle of incidence (i):** the angle between the incident ray and the normal. **Angle of reflection (r):** the angle between the reflected ray and the normal.

pages.title: The two laws of reflection
pages.body:
First Law: The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal to the surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

Second Law: The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.

Written as: i = r

pages.title: Basic calculations on reflection
pages.body:
Example 1: A ray of light strikes a mirror at an angle of incidence of 40°. What is the angle of reflection?

By the second law of reflection: angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 40°

Example 2: A ray of light hits a mirror and the angle between the incident ray and the mirror surface is 30°. What is the angle of incidence? What is the angle of reflection?

The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, not the surface. If the ray makes 30° with the surface, it makes 90° − 30° = 60° with the normal. So the angle of incidence = 60°. By the 2nd law, angle of reflection = 60°.

Example 3: What is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray if the angle of incidence is 35°?

Angle between incident and reflected ray = i + r = 35° + 35° = 70°

pages.body:
> **DEFINITION** **Refraction:** the bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium into another of different optical density (different speed of light). **Optical density:** a measure of how much a medium slows down light. A denser optical medium slows light more and causes more bending.

When light travels from one medium to another, it changes speed. This change in speed causes the light to change direction (unless it hits the boundary at 90°, in which case it passes straight through without bending).

pages.title: Total Internal Reflection
pages.body: When light is travelling from a denser medium (like glass or water) into a less dense medium (like air), it bends away from the normal. As the angle of incidence increases, the refracted ray bends more and more. At a certain angle, called the critical angle, the refracted ray travels exactly along the boundary surface. Beyond this critical angle, no light escapes into the less dense medium at all. All the light is reflected back into the denser medium. This is total internal reflection.

> **DEFINITION** **Critical angle:** the specific angle of incidence (inside the denser medium) at which the refracted ray travels along the boundary. Beyond this angle, total internal reflection occurs. **Total internal reflection:** when light hits the boundary inside a denser medium at an angle greater than the critical angle, and all the light is reflected back inside the denser medium.

Practical applications of total internal reflection:

- Optical fibres: glass fibres carry light signals (telephone, internet and TV data) over long distances with very low loss, because the light keeps bouncing internally all the way along the fibre.
- Diamonds: the critical angle of diamond is very small. Light entering a diamond undergoes total internal reflection many times before emerging, making diamonds sparkle brilliantly.
- Periscopes and binoculars: glass prisms use total internal reflection to redirect light through right angles without any loss.
- Medical endoscopes: optical fibres allow doctors to see inside the body without surgery.

pages.title: Dispersion of light
pages.body:
White light is not a single colour. It is a mixture of all the colours of the visible spectrum. When white light enters a glass prism (or any transparent medium), each colour is refracted by a slightly different amount because each has a slightly different speed. Violet light is slowed the most and bends the most; red light is slowed the least and bends the least. This separates the colours, producing a spectrum.

The colours of the visible spectrum in order, from least-bent to most-bent, are:

Red → Orange → Yellow → Green → Blue → Indigo → Violet

These can be remembered with the name ROY G BIV.

pages.title: How a rainbow forms
pages.body: A rainbow is a natural dispersion of sunlight. When sunlight enters a water droplet in the air, it refracts on entering, undergoes partial total internal reflection inside the droplet, and refracts again on leaving. Each colour exits at a slightly different angle, spreading the colours out. You see a rainbow when the Sun is behind you and rain is in front of you, so that the dispersed light from millions of droplets reaches your eyes.
